title: Deep eutectic solvent
wikitext:
{{Short description|Solutions of Lewis or Brønsted acids and bases}}
'''Deep eutectic solvents''' ('''DESs''') are solutions of [[Lewis acid|Lewis]] or [[Brønsted acid]]s and bases which form a [[Eutectic system|eutectic mixture]].<ref name="Smith14">{{cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=Emma L. |last2=Abbott |first2=Andrew P. |last3=Ryder |first3=Karl S. |title=Deep Eutectic Solvents (DESs) and Their Applications |journal=Chemical Reviews |date=12 November 2014 |volume=114 |issue=21 |pages=11060–11082 |doi=10.1021/cr300162p |pmid=25300631 |doi-access=free |hdl=2381/37428 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Deep eutectic solvents are highly tunable through varying the structure or relative ratio of parent components and thus have a wide variety of potential applications including catalytic, separation, and electrochemical processes.<ref name="Smith14" /><ref name="Gurkan19" /> The parent components of deep eutectic solvents engage in a complex hydrogen bonding network, which results in significant freezing point depression as compared to the parent compounds.<ref>{{cite web|title=Deep Eutectic Solvents|url=http://wet.kuleuven.be/english/summerschools/ionicliquids/lectures/abbott.pdf|website=kuleuven.be|publisher=University of Leicester|access-date=17 June 2014}}</ref> The extent of freezing point depression observed in DESs is well illustrated by a mixture of [[choline chloride]] (ChCl) and [[urea]] in a 1:2 [[mole (chemistry)|mole]] ratio. Choline chloride and urea are both solids at room temperature with melting points of 302 °C (decomposition point) and 133 °C respectively, yet the combination of the two in a 1:2 molar ratio forms a liquid with a freezing point of 12 °C.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abbott |first1=Andrew P. |last2=Capper |first2=Glen |last3=Davies |first3=David L. |last4=Rasheed |first4=Raymond K. |last5=Tambyrajah |first5=Vasuki |title=Novel solvent properties of choline chloride/urea mixtures |journal=Chemical Communications |date=19 December 2003 |issue=1 |pages=70–71 |doi=10.1039/b210714g |pmid=12610970 |hdl=2381/570 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> DESs share similar properties to ionic liquids such as tunability and lack of flammability yet are distinct in that ionic liquids are neat salts composed exclusively of discrete ions.<ref name="Smith14" /> In contrast to ordinary solvents, such as [[volatile organic compound]]s, DESs are non-flammable, and possess low vapour pressures and toxicity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=García |first1=Gregorio |last2=Aparicio |first2=Santiago |last3=Ullah |first3=Ruh |last4=Atilhan |first4=Mert |title=Deep Eutectic Solvents: Physicochemical Properties and Gas Separation Applications |journal=Energy & Fuels |date=16 April 2015 |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=2616–2644 |doi=10.1021/ef5028873 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Wide spread practical use of DESs in industrial process or devices has thus far been hindered by relatively high viscosities and low ionic conductivities. Additionally, lack of understanding of the relationship between parent compound structure and solvent function has prevented development of general design rules. Work to understand structure-function relation is on-going.

== Chemical classes ==

=== Four-class classification ===
DESs can be classified on the basis of their composition:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zdanowicz |first1=Magdalena |last2=Wilpiszewska |first2=Katarzyna |last3=Spychaj |first3=Tadeusz |title=Deep eutectic solvents for polysaccharides processing. A review |journal=Carbohydrate Polymers |date=November 2018 |volume=200 |pages=361–380 |doi=10.1016/j.carbpol.2018.07.078}}</ref><ref name="AbbottAl-Barzinjy2014" />

{| class="wikitable"
|-
!  !! Hydrogen bond acceptor !! Hydrogen bond donor
|-
! scope=row | Type 1 (I)
| Organic cation salt || Metal salt

This classification is an extension of the traditional scheme, in which the "organic cation" was limited to a [[Quaternary ammonium cation|quaternary ammonium]] and the "metal salt" was limited to chlorides.<ref name=Abbott07>{{cite journal |last1=Abbott |first1=Andrew P. |last2=Barron |first2=John C. |last3=Ryder |first3=Karl S. |last4=Wilson |first4=David |title=Eutectic-Based Ionic Liquids with Metal-Containing Anions and Cations |journal=Chemistry: A European Journal |date=27 July 2007 |volume=13 |issue=22 |pages=6495–6501 |doi=10.1002/chem.200601738 |pmid=17477454 }}</ref>

# Type 1 eutectics include a wide range of [[chlorometallate]] ionic solvents which were widely studied in the 1980s, such as imidazolium chloroaluminates which are based on mixtures of AlCl<sub>3</sub> + 1-Ethyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilkes |first1=John S. |last2=Levisky |first2=Joseph A. |last3=Wilson |first3=Robert A. |last4=Hussey |first4=Charles L. |title=Dialkylimidazolium chloroaluminate melts: a new class of room-temperature ionic liquids for electrochemistry, spectroscopy and synthesis |journal=Inorganic Chemistry |date=March 1982 |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=1263–1264 |doi=10.1021/ic00133a078 }}</ref> When chlorides are used, the metal can be Zn, Sn, Fe, Al, or Ga.<ref name=Abbott07/>
# Type 2 eutectics are similar to type 1, except that the hydrated form of the metal halide is used.  When chlorides are used, the metal can be Cr, Co, Cu, Ni, or Fe.<ref name=Abbott07/>
# Type 3 eutectics consist of hydrogen bond acceptors such as quaternary ammonium salts (e.g. choline chloride) and hydrogen bond donors (e.g urea, [[ethylene glycol]]). Many of them are ''metal-free deep eutectic solvents''.<ref name="Gurkan19">{{cite journal |last1=Gurkan |first1=Burcu |last2=Squire |first2=Henry |last3=Pentzer |first3=Emily |title=Metal-Free Deep Eutectic Solvents: Preparation, Physical Properties, and Significance |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters |date=19 December 2019 |volume=10 |issue=24 |pages=7956–7964 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpclett.9b01980 |pmid=31804088 |osti=1608304 |s2cid=208643425 |url=https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1608304 }}</ref><ref name="AbbottAl-Barzinjy2014">{{cite journal |last1=Abbott |first1=Andrew P. |last2=Al-Barzinjy |first2=Azeez A. |last3=Abbott |first3=Paul D. |last4=Frisch |first4=Gero |last5=Harris |first5=Robert C. |last6=Hartley |first6=Jennifer |last7=Ryder |first7=Karl S. |title=Speciation, physical and electrolytic properties of eutectic mixtures based on CrCl3·6H2O and urea |journal=Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics |date=2014 |volume=16 |issue=19 |pages=9047–9055 |doi=10.1039/c4cp00057a |pmid=24695874 |bibcode=2014PCCP...16.9047A |url=https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/10125527 |doi-access=free |hdl=2381/37718 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Type 3 eutectics have been successfully used in metal processing applications such as electrodeposition, [[electropolishing]], and metal extraction.
# Type 4 eutectics use a metal salt as the HBA and an organic HBD. It was originally thought to be a hybrid between type 1 and type 3, but then it was found that it had some properties of its own: for example, urea can form a type 4 DES with the chloride of Zn, Sn, and Fe (III), but not with Al.<ref name=Abbott07/> Type 4 eutectics are of interest for electrodeposition as they produce cationic metal complexes, ensuring that the double layer close to the electrode surface has a high metal ion concentration.<ref name="AbbottAl-Barzinjy2014" />

=== Natural deep eutectic solvents ===
Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES) are deep eutectic solvents which are composed of two or more compounds that are generally  [[primary metabolite]]s, i.e. [[organic acid]]s, [[sugar]]s, [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohols]], [[amine]]s and [[amino acid]]s. The classical example is the combination of ChCl and carboxylic acids.<ref name=Abbott04>{{cite journal |last1=Abbott |first1=Andrew P. |last2=Boothby |first2=David |last3=Capper |first3=Glen |last4=Davies |first4=David L. |last5=Rasheed |first5=Raymond K. |title=Deep Eutectic Solvents Formed between Choline Chloride and Carboxylic Acids: Versatile Alternatives to Ionic Liquids |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=July 2004 |volume=126 |issue=29 |pages=9142–9147 |doi=10.1021/ja048266j |pmid=15264850 }}</ref> Almost all known NADES are metal-free and type 3. Being made from cheap, abundant, and nontoxic biomolecules, there is considerable interest in their application in the lab and in industry.<ref name=Dai13>{{cite journal |last1=Dai |first1=Yuntao |last2=van Spronsen |first2=Jaap |last3=Witkamp |first3=Geert-Jan |last4=Verpoorte |first4=Robert |last5=Choi |first5=Young Hae |title=Ionic Liquids and Deep Eutectic Solvents in Natural Products Research: Mixtures of Solids as Extraction Solvents |journal=Journal of Natural Products |date=22 November 2013 |volume=76 |issue=11 |pages=2162–2173 |doi=10.1021/np400051w |pmid=24188074 |hdl-access=free |hdl=1887/3193548 |s2cid=5813169 }}</ref>

NADES are also biologically interesting as they can plausibly form in living cells. Alongside natural [[ionic liquid]]s, they may represent a type of liquid phase separate from water and lipids. They serve as a potential explanation to so-called "glass formation" of sugars.<ref name="choi11">{{cite journal |last1=Choi |first1=Young Hae |last2=van Spronsen |first2=Jaap |last3=Dai |first3=Yuntao |last4=Verberne |first4=Marianne |last5=Hollmann |first5=Frank |last6=Arends |first6=Isabel W.C.E. |last7=Witkamp |first7=Geert-Jan |last8=Verpoorte |first8=Robert |title=Are Natural Deep Eutectic Solvents the Missing Link in Understanding Cellular Metabolism and Physiology? |journal=Plant Physiology |date=August 2011 |volume=156 |issue=4 |pages=1701–1705 |doi=10.1104/pp.111.178426 |pmid=21677097 |pmc=3149944 }}</ref><ref name=Dai13b>{{cite journal |last1=Dai |first1=Yuntao |last2=van Spronsen |first2=Jaap |last3=Witkamp |first3=Geert-Jan |last4=Verpoorte |first4=Robert |last5=Choi |first5=Young Hae |title=Natural deep eutectic solvents as new potential media for green technology |journal=Analytica Chimica Acta |date=March 2013 |volume=766 |pages=61–68 |doi=10.1016/j.aca.2012.12.019 |pmid=23427801 |hdl=1887/3193533 |s2cid=19255174 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Some eutectic solvents are formed by complete drying of biological fluids. For example, completely drying [[maple syrup]] leaves a liquid consisting of mostly Suc [sucrose] and [[malic acid]]; lab work shows that the ideal DES mixture for these two substances is at 1:1 molar ratio. ''[[Cleome hassleriana]]'' nectar (mostly Glu [glucose], Fru [fructose], Suc) remains a fluid when completely dried; lab work shows that the most stable DES made from these three substances is at a 1:1:1 molar ratio.<ref name="choi11"/> Also of biological interest is the formation of water-containing DESs using Glu, Fru, or Suc at 1:1:1 molar ratio with ChCl and water. Here the water is strongly retained in the liquid and cannot be [[Evaporation|evaporated]].<ref name="choi11"/>

== Chemical research ==
{{anchor|research}}
Compared to modern [[ionic liquid]]s based on discrete anions, such as [[bistriflimide]], which share many characteristics but are ionic compounds and not ionic mixtures, DES are cheaper to make and sometimes [[biodegradation|biodegradable]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Clarke |first1=Coby J. |last2=Tu |first2=Wei-Chien |last3=Levers |first3=Oliver |last4=Bröhl |first4=Andreas |last5=Hallett |first5=Jason P. |title=Green and Sustainable Solvents in Chemical Processes |journal=Chemical Reviews |date=24 January 2018 |volume=118 |issue=2 |pages=747–800 |doi=10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00571 |pmid=29300087 |hdl=10044/1/59694 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Therefore, DES can be used as safe, efficient, simple, and low–cost solvents.

To date, there are numerous applications that have been studied for DES. By varying the components of the DES and their molar ratios, new DES can be produced. For this reason, many new applications are presented in the literature every year.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Svigelj |first1=Rossella |last2=Dossi |first2=Nicolò |last3=Grazioli |first3=Cristian |last4=Toniolo |first4=Rosanna |title=Deep Eutectic Solvents (DESs) and Their Application in Biosensor Development |journal=Sensors |date=January 2021 |volume=21 |issue=13 |page=4263 |doi=10.3390/s21134263 |pmid=34206344 |pmc=8271379 |bibcode=2021Senso..21.4263S |language=en|doi-access=free }}</ref> Some of the earliest applications of DES were the electrofinishing of metals using DES as electrolytes.<ref name="AbbottMcKenzie2007">{{cite book |doi=10.1021/bk-2007-0975.ch013 |chapter=Electropolishing and Electroplating of Metals Using Ionic Liquids Based on Choline Chloride |title=Ionic Liquids IV |series=ACS Symposium Series |year=2007 |last1=Abbott |first1=Andrew P. |last2=McKenzie |first2=Katy J. |last3=Ryder |first3=Karl S. |volume=975 |pages=186–197 |isbn=978-0-8412-7445-7 }}</ref> [[Organic compound]]s such as [[benzoic acid]] (solubility  0.82 mol/L) have great solubility in DES, and this even includes [[cellulose]].<ref>{{cite patent |inventor=Richard F. Miller |pubdate=2010 |title=Deep eutectic solvents and applications |status=Patent |number= 8022014 |fdate= Mar 25, 2009 |gdate=Sep 20, 2011 |country=US}}</ref> For this reason, DES were applied as extraction solvents for such material from their complex matrices. DES as extraction solvents in the separation of aromatic hydrocarbons from [[naphtha]] was also studied and promising results were published in 2012<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kareem |first1=Mukhtar A. |last2=Mjalli |first2=Farouq S. |last3=Hashim |first3=Mohd Ali |last4=Hadj-Kali |first4=Mohamed K. O. |last5=Bagh |first5=Fatemeh Saadat Ghareh |last6=Alnashef |first6=Inas M. |title=Phase equilibria of toluene/heptane with tetrabutylphosphonium bromide based deep eutectic solvents for the potential use in the separation of aromatics from naphtha |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |date=15 November 2012 |volume=333 |pages=47–54 |doi=10.1016/j.fluid.2012.07.020 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kareem |first1=Mukhtar A. |last2=Mjalli |first2=Farouq S. |last3=Hashim |first3=Mohd Ali |last4=AlNashef |first4=Inas M. |title=Liquid–liquid equilibria for the ternary system (phosphonium based deep eutectic solvent–benzene–hexane) at different temperatures: A new solvent introduced |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |date=25 January 2012 |volume=314 |pages=52–59 |doi=10.1016/j.fluid.2011.10.024 }}</ref> and 2013.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kareem |first1=Mukhtar A. |last2=Mjalli |first2=Farouq S. |last3=Hashim |first3=Mohd Ali |last4=Hadj-Kali |first4=Mohamed K. O. |last5=Ghareh Bagh |first5=Fatemeh Saadat |last6=Alnashef |first6=Inas M. |title=Phase equilibria of toluene/heptane with deep eutectic solvents based on ethyltriphenylphosphonium iodide for the potential use in the separation of aromatics from naphtha |journal=The Journal of Chemical Thermodynamics |date=1 October 2013 |volume=65 |pages=138–149 |doi=10.1016/j.jct.2013.05.046 }}</ref>

They were also studied for their applicability in the production and purification of biodiesel,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hayyan |first1=Maan |last2=Mjalli |first2=Farouq S. |last3=Hashim |first3=Mohd Ali |last4=AlNashef |first4=Inas M. |title=A novel technique for separating glycerine from palm oil-based biodiesel using ionic liquids |journal=Fuel Processing Technology |date=January 2010 |volume=91 |issue=1 |pages=116–120 |doi=10.1016/j.fuproc.2009.09.002 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hayyan |first1=Adeeb |last2=Hashim |first2=Mohd Ali |last3=Hayyan |first3=Maan |last4=Mjalli |first4=Farouq S. |last5=AlNashef |first5=Inas M. |title=A novel ammonium based eutectic solvent for the treatment of free fatty acid and synthesis of biodiesel fuel |journal=Industrial Crops and Products |date=April 2013 |volume=46 |pages=392–398 |doi=10.1016/j.indcrop.2013.01.033 }}</ref> and their ability to extract metals for analysis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Habibi |first1=Emadaldin |last2=Ghanemi |first2=Kamal |last3=Fallah-Mehrjardi |first3=Mehdi |last4=Dadolahi-Sohrab |first4=Ali |title=A novel digestion method based on a choline chloride–oxalic acid deep eutectic solvent for determining Cu, Fe, and Zn in fish samples |journal=Analytica Chimica Acta |date=January 2013 |volume=762 |pages=61–67 |doi=10.1016/j.aca.2012.11.054 |pmid=23327946 }}</ref>  Incorporating microwave heating with deep eutectic solvent can efficiently increase the solubility power of DES and reduce the time required for complete dissolution of biological samples at [[atmospheric pressure]].<ref name="GhanemiNavidi2014">{{cite journal |last1=Ghanemi |first1=Kamal |last2=Navidi |first2=Mohammad-Amin |last3=Fallah-Mehrjardi |first3=Mehdi |last4=Dadolahi-Sohrab |first4=Ali |title=Ultra-fast microwave-assisted digestion in choline chloride–oxalic acid deep eutectic solvent for determining Cu, Fe, Ni and Zn in marine biological samples |journal=Anal. Methods |date=2014 |volume=6 |issue=6 |pages=1774–1781 |doi=10.1039/C3AY41843J }}</ref> It is noteworthy that proton-conducting DES (e.g. the mixture of imidazolium methanesulfonate and 1H-1,2,4-triazole in a 1:3 mole ratio or the mixture of 1,2,4-triazolium methanesulfonate and 1H-1,2,4-triazole in a 1:3 mole ratio, wherein the Brønsted base may act as the hydrogen bond donor) have also found applications as proton conductors for fuel cells.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Luo |first1=Jiangshui |last2=Tan |first2=Tran Van |last3=Conrad |first3=Olaf |last4=Vankelecom |first4=Ivo F. J. |last7=Agert |first7=Carsten |last8=Conrad |first8=Olaf |title=Protic ionic liquid and ionic melts prepared from methanesulfonic acid and 1H-1,2,4-triazole as high temperature PEMFC electrolytes |journal=Journal of Materials Chemistry |date=2011 |volume=21 |issue=28 |page=10426 |doi=10.1039/C0JM04306K |url=https://lirias.kuleuven.be/handle/123456789/313759 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Emulsions ===
Owing to their unique composition, DES are promising solvating environments, affecting the structure and self-assembly of solutes. For example, the self-assembly of [[sodium dodecyl sulfate]] (SDS) in DES has recently been studied, implying DES can form microemulsions different from those in water.<ref name="Pal_2016">{{cite journal |last1=Pal |first1=Mahi |last2=Rai |first2=Rewa |last3=Yadav |first3=Anita |last4=Khanna |first4=Rajesh |last5=Baker |first5=Gary A. |last6=Pandey |first6=Siddharth |title=Self-Aggregation of Sodium Dodecyl Sulfate within (Choline Chloride + Urea) Deep Eutectic Solvent |journal=Langmuir |date=11 November 2014 |volume=30 |issue=44 |pages=13191–13198 |doi=10.1021/la5035678 |pmid=25314953 }}</ref> In another case, the solvation of the polymer [[polyvinylpyrrolidone]] (PVP) in DES is distinct from water, whereby the DES appear to be a better solvent for the polymer.<ref name="Sapir_2016">{{cite journal |last1=Sapir |first1=Liel |last2=Stanley |first2=Christopher B. |last3=Harries |first3=Daniel |title=Properties of Polyvinylpyrrolidone in a Deep Eutectic Solvent |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A |date=19 May 2016 |volume=120 |issue=19 |pages=3253–3259 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpca.5b11927 |pmid=26963367 |bibcode=2016JPCA..120.3253S |osti=1424493 }}</ref> It has been also shown that depending on [[state of matter]] of the solute [[homogeneous]] or [[heterogeneous]] mixtures are formed.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Häkkinen |first1=Riina |last2=Alshammari |first2=Odeh |last3=Timmermann |first3=Vanessa |last4=D'Agostino |first4=Carmine |last5=Abbott |first5=Andrew |title=Nanoscale Clustering of Alcoholic Solutes in Deep Eutectic Solvents Studied by |url=https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/nanoscale-clustering-of-alcoholic-solutes-in-deep-eutectic-solvents-studied-by-nuclear-magnetic-resonance-and-dynamic-light-scattering(26d06faf-faad-4f04-89f9-e38af3238f6c).html }}</ref>

=== Ore ===
DES have also been studied for their potential use as more environmentally sustainable solvents for extracting gold and other precious metals from [[ore]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Jenkin|first1=Gawen R.T.|last2=Al-Bassam|first2=Ahmed Z.M.|last3=Harris|first3=Robert C.|last4=Abbott|first4=Andrew P.|last5=Smith|first5=Daniel J.|last6=Holwell|first6=David A.|last7=Chapman|first7=Robert J.|last8=Stanley|first8=Christopher J.|title=The application of deep eutectic solvent ionic liquids for environmentally-friendly dissolution and recovery of precious metals|journal=Minerals Engineering|date=March 2016|volume=87|pages=18–24|doi=10.1016/j.mineng.2015.09.026|bibcode=2016MiEng..87...18J |doi-access=free|hdl=10141/603645|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Some solvent extraction work has been done using DES solvents, Mark Foreman at [[Chalmers University of Technology|Chalmers]] has in recent years published several papers on this topic. He wrote about the use of the solvents for [[battery recycling]] from an applied point of view<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Albler |first1=Franziska-Jane |last2=Bica |first2=Katharina |last3=Foreman |first3=Mark R. StJ. |last4=Holgersson |first4=Stellan |last5=Tyumentsev |first5=Mikhail S. |title=A comparison of two methods of recovering cobalt from a deep eutectic solvent: Implications for battery recycling |journal=Journal of Cleaner Production |date=20 November 2017 |volume=167 |pages=806–814 |doi=10.1016/j.jclepro.2017.08.135 }}</ref> and he also published what may be the first ever serious study of solvent extraction of metals from DES.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Foreman |first1=Mark R.StJ. |title=Progress towards a process for the recycling of nickel metal hydride electric cells using a deep eutectic solvent |journal=Cogent Chemistry |date=31 December 2016 |volume=2 |issue=1 |article-number=1139289 |doi=10.1080/23312009.2016.1139289 |s2cid=21834215 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Foreman has also published two pure research papers on the [[Thermodynamic activity|activity]] issues in DES, in the first<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Foreman |first1=Mark R. St J. |last2=Holgersson |first2=Stellan |last3=McPhee |first3=Conor |last4=Tyumentsev |first4=Mikhail S. |title=Activity coefficients in deep eutectic solvents: implications for the solvent extraction of metals |journal=New Journal of Chemistry |date=29 January 2018 |volume=42 |issue=3 |pages=2006–2012 |doi=10.1039/C7NJ03736H }}</ref> he pointed out that activity coefficients in DES do appear to deviate wildly away from their values in [[sodium chloride]] solution while in his later paper<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cen |first1=Peng |last2=Spahiu |first2=Kastriot |last3=Tyumentsev |first3=Mikhail S. |last4=Foreman |first4=Mark R. St. J. |title=Metal extraction from a deep eutectic solvent, an insight into activities |journal=Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics |date=2020 |volume=22 |issue=19 |pages=11012–11024 |doi=10.1039/C9CP05982B |pmid=32367089 |bibcode=2020PCCP...2211012C |s2cid=218504859 |doi-access=free }}</ref> he provides a mathematical model for the activity coefficients in DES using the [[SIT equation]]. Lastly, DES involvement in thermoelectrical field was researched through the incorporation of DES in thermoelectric polymer for the synthesis of improved thermoelectric polymer films.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rahman |first1=Shahriar Mufid |last2=Mohd Said |first2=Suhana Binti |last3=Subramanian |first3=Balamurugan |last4=Long |first4=Bui Duc |last5=Kareem |first5=Mukhtar A. |last6=Soin |first6=Norhayati |title=Synthesis and Characterization of Polymer Electrolyte Using Deep Eutectic Solvents and Electrospun Poly(vinyl alcohol) Membrane |journal=Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research |date=3 August 2016 |volume=55 |issue=30 |pages=8341–8348 |doi=10.1021/acs.iecr.6b01754 }}</ref>

== In biology ==
Both individual DES components and the resultant mixtures have shown to be highly biodegradable.<ref name=Wazeer17>{{Cite journal |last1=Wazeer |first1=Irfan |last2=Hayyan |first2=Maan |last3=Hadj-Kali |first3=Mohamed K |date=2017 |title=Deep eutectic solvents: designer fluids for chemical processes |journal=Journal of Chemical Technology & Biotechnology |volume=93 |issue=4 |pages=945–958 |doi=10.1002/jctb.5491 |issn=0268-2575 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Individual DES components are generally non-toxic. However, their combination into a DES produces a higher toxicity for bacteria, fungi, fish, ''[[Artemia]]'' (brime shrimp)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hayyan |first1=Maan |last2=Hashim |first2=Mohd Ali |last3=Hayyan |first3=Adeeb |last4=Al-Saadi |first4=Mohammed A. |last5=AlNashef |first5=Inas M. |last6=Mirghani |first6=Mohamed E.S. |last7=Saheed |first7=Olorunnisola Kola |date=2013 |title=Are deep eutectic solvents benign or toxic? |journal=Chemosphere |volume=90 |issue=7 |pages=2193–2195 |bibcode=2013Chmsp..90.2193H |doi=10.1016/j.chemosphere.2012.11.004 |issn=0045-6535 |pmid=23200570}}</ref>, ''Hydra'', and cultured mammal cells compared to the individual components; a case of [[synergy]].<ref name=Wazeer17>{{Cite journal |last1=Wazeer |first1=Irfan |last2=Hayyan |first2=Maan |last3=Hadj-Kali |first3=Mohamed K |date=2017 |title=Deep eutectic solvents: designer fluids for chemical processes |journal=Journal of Chemical Technology & Biotechnology |volume=93 |issue=4 |pages=945–958 |doi=10.1002/jctb.5491 |issn=0268-2575 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The toxicity of DES to naked, individual cells is a natural consequence of its physiochemical properties: what allows it to work as a good solvent also enables it to disrupt [[cell membrane]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mbous |first1=Yves Paul |last2=Hayyan |first2=Maan |last3=Wong |first3=Won Fen |last4=Hayyan |first4=Adeeb |last5=Looi |first5=Chung Yeng |last6=Hashim |first6=Mohd Ali |title=Simulation of Deep Eutectic Solvents’ Interaction with Membranes of Cancer Cells Using COSMO-RS |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B |date=15 October 2020 |volume=124 |issue=41 |pages=9086–9094 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcb.0c04801}}</ref>

The ability of DES to increase the permeability of [[lipid bilayer]] membranes leads to applications in [[biocatalysis]]. When living microbes are grown for producing chemicals, a common bottleneck is the permeability of their cell membranes limiting the flux of substrates and products. Adding a small amount of DES to the [[growth medium]] solves this problem: just a 1% (v/v) addition of a (NA)DES based on [[choline acetate]] increases the isoeugenol-to-vanillin bioconversion yield of ''Lysinibacillus fusiformis'' 142%.<ref name=IMH19>{{cite journal |last1=Ibn Majdoub Hassani |first1=Fatima Zohra |last2=Amzazi |first2=Saaid |last3=Lavandera |first3=Iván |title=The Versatile Applications of DES and Their Influence on Oxidoreductase-Mediated Transformations |journal=Molecules (Basel, Switzerland) |date=11 June 2019 |volume=24 |issue=11 |pages=2190 |pmid=31212686 |doi=10.3390/molecules24112190|doi-access=free}}</ref> DES also acts in membrane-independent ways, directly acting on the enzymes to modify its behavior (e.g. increase stersoselectivity). This can be applied to live cells and their dead components alike.<ref name=IMH19/> Some enzymes even work in water-free conditions where DES is the only solvent.<ref name="choi11"/>

extract:
Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are solutions of Lewis or Brønsted acids and bases which form a eutectic mixture. Deep eutectic solvents are highly tunable through varying the structure or relative ratio of parent components and thus have a wide variety of potential applications including catalytic, separation, and electrochemical processes. The parent components of deep eutectic solvents engage in a complex hydrogen bonding network, which results in significant freezing point depression as compared to the parent compounds. The extent of freezing point depression observed in DESs is well illustrated by a mixture of choline chloride (ChCl) and urea in a 1:2 mole ratio. Choline chloride and urea are both solids at room temperature with melting points of 302 °C (decomposition point) and 133 °C respectively, yet the combination of the two in a 1:2 molar ratio forms a liquid with a freezing point of 12 °C. DESs share similar properties to ionic liquids such as tunability and lack of flammability yet are distinct in that ionic liquids are neat salts composed exclusively of discrete ions. In contrast to ordinary solvents, such as volatile organic compounds, DESs are non-flammable, and possess low vapour pressures and toxicity.
Wide spread practical use of DESs in industrial process or devices has thus far been hindered by relatively high viscosities and low ionic conductivities. Additionally, lack of understanding of the relationship between parent compound structure and solvent function has prevented development of general design rules. Work to understand structure-function relation is on-going.
